The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing the appellants from the property known as Palmar Oiteral. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit for mere declaration simpliciter could not lie. The defendants, besides contending that the suit was barred on the principle of res judicata and/or constructive res judicata as found in Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure pleaded that on the expiry of the lease at the end of December, 1967 the lease stood terminated by efflux of time and defendant No. 2 was entitled to let out the property to defendant No. 1 and hence the latter was in lawful possession of the said property. The defendants contended that the suit had been filed within the period of lease and the plaintiff was entitled to get possession of the property from the defendants. The Trial Court upheld the contention of the defendants that the property was demised to him and he was the lawful tenant thereof till his possession came to be disturbed sometime in June, 1968. The Trial court held that the plaintiff had paid a sum of Rs. 1200 to defendant No 2 through his employee Dattu Kenkro by way of advance rent for the year commencing from January 1, 1968. the date of the expiry of lease at the beginning of December,1967 and the first installment of 1968 but the owner, defendant No.2, in collusion with defendant No.1 executed a deed of lease in favour of the latter effective from January 1. 1968 without his tenancy having been lawfully terminated. The Trial Judge held that the suit of the plaintiff was not barred by res judicata as well as by constructive res judicata. The First Appellate Court concurred with the findings recorded by the Trial Court and dismissed the appeal. The First Appeal No. 82/85 was allowed by the High Court on the ground of res judicata. Hence this appeal by the legal representatives. The appellants contended that the courts below had applied the wrong test and had based their findings on the question of tenancy and dispossession on mere conjectures. It was submitted that the courts had applied the correct test and had proceeded on the basis that the suit property was demised and the plaintiff had been in lawful possession thereof till his eviction. The High Court, therefore, held that the decree passed by the Civil Court was unsustainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question of tenancy is a mixed question of law

The appellant, who was the sole executor of the will, claimed to have been executed by one G, a daughter of the testator, on August 22, 1945, in favour of the respondents 2 to 4 and his daughter, the other two daughters, and the appellant, who had been living with G, as his adopted son, under a will executed by G. The respondents 2 to 5 were the sons of G and the appellant 's daughter, and the respondents 2 and 4 were the sons and the appellant was the son of G. The appellant 's case was that under the will the respondents 2, to 4 and the appellant were entitled to dispose of the properties by a will and that the respondents 2 & 4 were entitled to execute the will in favour of G. On the question of the validity of the will the High Court held that the will was not proved to have been duly executed by G and that the will had not been proved to have come into existence at the time of the execution of the will. The High Court also held that the respondents 1 to 4 were not entitled to execute a will in favour G and that G was entitled to execute it in favour of his daughter G. The High court also held that G was not entitled to the properties in question in view of the provisions of section 68 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, and that the appellant ' was entitled to the entire properties in question. The High, Court also held in favour of respondent 1 and the appellant. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the will executed by the respondents 2. to 4 was not proved by the appellant and the will was duly registered. The will was not duly registered. Held, further, that the respondents ' case was that the will in question was not proved and the will had been duly registered. Held, also, that the High Court was not justified in recording the findings of the trial court on the question of due and valid execution of the wills. The appellants, who were manufacturing Arcic equipment, were manufacturing Arc carbons, which were used for the purpose of manufacturing electrical equipment, and were, therefore, liable to sales tax under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The sales tax authorities, relying on the decision of this Court in the State of Andhra Pradesh vs Srimathi Nidmarthi Saraswathi Devi, held that the appellants were liable to sales Tax under the Act. The High Court, in appeal, held that such a decision was not correct. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had erred in holding that the appellants ' products were covered by the relevant entry No. 4 of the Schedule to the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that these products were covered under the relevant entry. [567 B] (2) The High Courts were right in holding the appellants liable to salestax under the Andhra Act. [568 C] (3) The High court was right in its conclusion that the appellants are liable to sales. Tax under the Andhra State Act is a tax on the sale of goods. The taxable event is the sale of the goods. The goods are sold by the assessee to the consumers. The goods, therefore, are taxable under the Andhra General Sales Tax. [569 D] (4) The High. Court was right, in the facts and circumstances of the case, in holding that, the appellants were not liable to sales 'tax under the Act, because the goods were sold to the consumers by the assessee. [561 C] (5) The High, Court was right. [562 C] (6) The High 'Court was right in the view that the appellants had failed to establish that the goods were manufactured for use as an aid or addition. [563 D] (7) The High COurt was right in not taking the view that these products are not "goods" within the meaning of Entry No. 4 in Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh Act. [565 E] (8) The High Cour trate was right in saying that the goods manufactured were not "goods". [565 G] (9) The High Court was right. The High Co trict was right in observing that the goods are not "other goods" within the definition of the term in the Andhra Pradesh Sales Tax Act. [551 C]

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966, with effect from 1 7 1985, and a new rule which was introduced in the Gujarat Minor Minerals Rules 1966, with retrospective effect from 1 8 1985, on the ground that the said rule was ultra vires the State Legislature. The petitioners contended that the said notification was violative of the provisions of Article 301 of the Constitution and was void. The petitioners also contended that the State Legislature was not competent to enact the said rule and the notification was invalid. The petitioners further contended that the impugned notification was violative Of Article 301 of Constitution of India as it was not issued in the public interest and that the State Government had no power to issue the notification in question. The petitioners, therefore, prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to issue a notification in terms of the new rule which had been introduced in the year 1985 with retrospective effect. The petitioners prayed for a direction to the State Government not to issue the said notification. The petitioners in the writ petitions contended that the notification was violative and the State Government was not competent under the Act to issue the same. The petitioners urged that the State had no power under the Act, to issue the impugned notification, and that the notification issued by it was violative of Article 301. The petitioners submitted that the State was not competent in law to issue the aforesaid notification. The State Government had the power to issue it, and that it was not competent for the State Government, to issue it. The petitioners therefore prayed for a mandamus directing the Government to issue the Notification in terms of a new rule. The petitioners ' writ petitions were dismissed by the High Court. The petitioners have filed these petitions for special leave to appeal against the decision of the High Court, contending that the State has no power to amend the Gujarat Minor Rules, 1966 and the notification issued in the year 1986 was violative of Articles 301 and 301 of the constitution of India. Dismissing the petitions, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The State Legislature is competent to enact a law with retrospective effect and the notification is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [413B] 2. The State cannot issue a notification under the Act in the public interests. The State has the power to make a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the Act under which the Rules are made. [414C] 3. The State is not competent to issue the notifications in the public Interest. [415C]

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. For the subsequent years the amounts received were assessed to income tax in the hands of the respondents under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Income tax Act. The assessments were for the assessment years 1951 52, 1952 53, 1953 54 and 1954 55. The assessments so made were for the assessments years 1950 51, 1951 52, 1953 54, and 1954 55 and were therefore for the assessment year 1951 52 to 1955 53. The assessments in respect of the years 1950 51 and 1951 52 were for the year 1951 52 and were for the subsequent years. The assessments for 1951 52 to 1954 55 were therefore quashed. The Commissioner of Income tax took an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal and the Tribunal held that assessment could not be made on Amarchand and that section 24B had no application to the income received after the death of Amarchand and was therefore not taxable. The High Court, on a reference, held that the notices under section 34 of the Income Tax Act could validly be served only for the assessment of the year 1950 51 and notices for the subsequent year were invalid. The Commissioner appealed to this Court. Held, that the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which had been held not to be liable to tax were those which were not received in the previous year and were therefore not liable to be taxed in the hands Of the heirs and legal representatives who cannot be deemed to be assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years. The assessees were not liable to tax in the years of assessment as the income of the deceased was not received in that year and was therefore taxable. The assessees had not been assessed to tax in respect of those years.

The appellant was convicted by the Additional Sessions judge, Bulandshahr, for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and in two of the three cases, the appellant was convicted for offences under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant contended that the search was illegal because the search was not conducted in accordance with the provisions of section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and that the search and seizure were illegal. Held, that the search in the present case was illegal because it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code. The search was illegal as the appellant was in possession of the articles in question and the search was in contravention Of the provisions of the Code and the search and the seizure were illegal and the appellant was rightly convicted. The search and seizure of the articles were illegal because the appellant was not in possession of them. The search in the instant case was illegal as it was in violation of the provisions Of sections 103 and 166 of the Code, and the search could not be justified on the ground that the appellant had taken the articles in his possession.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302, I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the conviction and sentence. Held, that the High Court was wrong in rejecting the extra judicial confession of the appellant. The extra judicial confession was admissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the appellant made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied on by the High Court, was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai. The extrajudicial confession was admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act and the appellant was rightly convicted. The extra Judicial confession was admissible against the appellant as it was made to a police officer and was not made to a Magistrate. The extra-judicial confession was inadmissible in evidence as it was not made in the presence of the accused or the police officer. The extra examination of the accused was not admissible as it was inadmissible in the trial court. The extra evidence was inadmissible in view of the fact that the appellant was not produced before the Magistrate. The evidence of the appellant was inadmissible in material particulars and was not admissible in evidence. The extra enquiry was not admissible against the accused as it was a confession made to a person who was not produced. The extra investigation was not admissible under section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The extra examining of the accused could not be admissible against him as it was admissible against him.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation, was elected to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December, 1978. The final electoral roll was published on September 30, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963. The final roll was published in November, 1978. Thereafter the calendar of events was published on November 25, 1978 notifying that claims and objections which had not been preferred as required under the Rules would be rejected. The final publication of the electoral roll under Rule 8 of the Rules was done on November 25. The final published electoral roll was then published on November 26, 1978. After the respondents filed their counter affidavits, the petition was amended by the inclusion of an additional prayer that the declaration of the results of the election should also be quashed. After the respondent filed their counter affidavit, the petition came up for hearing and was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court on January 20, 1979. The appellants filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court and the same was dismissed on January 20. 1979. On December 30, 1978, the High Court dismissed the petition for special Leave. The appellants contended that the time for filing the counter affidavit was over and the writ petition was filed on December 28, 1978, and that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the petition on the ground that the writ petition itself was presented on December 28. 1978. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Court as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing it. The writ petition itself had been presented on December, 28, 1978. No satisfactory reason for the delay was set out in the petition. It is well settled that the power of the High court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation for delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. This rule applies also to a case in which the validity of an election to a local authority is challenged. The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under Article 226 is a matter within the discretion of the High Courts which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [493G H; 502A B]

The appellants were directors of a company. The balance sheet and the profit and loss accounts were laid before the general meeting. The appellants were prosecuted under section 133(3). The High Court, however, held that the appellants were liable under section 134(4) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellants were liable for the failure to attend general meeting. [427 D] (2) The section does not say that the failure to call a general meeting and to lay it before the general bodies meeting is made penal by the Act. The section does say that the company and its directors could not rely on their failure to call the general body meetings. [428 F G] (3) The section is a composite one which lays down various requirements which are to be complied with by the company under its first four sub clauses and sub cl. (5) is the penal sub section which penalises the failure to comply with any of the requirements contained in any of the four preceding sub sections. [429 G H] (4) The section in the English Act is a composite and not a composite one. The section is not a composite. It lays down various standards which are to he complied with by a company under its second four sub clauses. [431 A] (5) The section speaks of failure to call general meeting and does not say anything about the failure to do so. [432 B] (6) The section says nothing about the failure of the directors to call the meeting as a defence to the prosecution. [433 C] (7) The section has been enacted to give effect to the policy of the legislature. The object of the section is to give effect and not to give effect. The section has to be read as a whole and it is not necessary to set out the sections in extenso. [434 D] (8) The section cannot be read as laying down any general principle of law. It is not necessary that the section should be read as providing a general principle of general application. It is sufficient if it is read as providing that the failure of a director to call a meeting would be an offence. The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them, and the appellants were put in possession of the mills and the factory. The appellants were put into possession of the mill and the factory was leased to the appellants for five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants contended that the lease was illegal and void as it was not executed in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Held, that the notice under section 12 of the Act was valid and the appellants could not be evicted. The notice was valid and it was not necessary to issue the notice under the section. The notice did not purport to be a notice under section 10 of the Act and the appellants had no right to challenge it. The notice could not be said to be invalid merely because it was issued in pursuance of a direction given by the Custodian under section 10. The notice in terms refers to the leases granted by the evacuee and not to the mortgages. The notice is not a notice under the Act and could not be challenged in a court of law. The notice under section 9 of the Act is not a mere formality and it is not a condition precedent to the exercise of the power of the Custodian under the Act. The notice must be held to be valid and the notice must be deemed to be valid. The notice can be challenged in any court of law and the question whether the notice is valid or not is a question of fact to be determined by the Custodian and not by the Court. The notice may be served by the Custodian himself or by some one authorised by him in that behalf and the notice may be sent to the appellants at their registered address. The notice need not be in the form prescribed by the Act and it can be served by any one of the modes prescribed by it. The notices can be served in the manner prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure. The notice cannot be said to have been served in the way prescribed by the provisions of section 10 of Act. The notices are not invalid merely because they are not in the form required by the Act.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of former Dholpur state into the Matsya Union. The suit out of which the appeal arose was filed by the respondent against the State of Rajasthan. The respondent was a citizen of the former State of Dholpur and the State of Jaipur was merged in the State of Madhya Pradesh on January 26, 1950. The respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni and 20 seers of chuni before December 2, 1947. The respondent deposited Rs. 30,000 as export duty in advance. The permit had been granted on June 28, 1947 and remained in force upto December 2,1947. The respondent did not export the entire quantity of the commodity before December 2. 1947. Thereafter he applied for refund of the amount. The suit was filed in January 1952. The respondent claimed refund of the entire amount. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court held that the respondent was entitled to refund of the excess amount. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The respondent was not bound by any obligation against the old sovereign of the former Rajasthan State of Dholapur. The new sovereign was not bound to refund the amount. [186D] (ii) The respondent could not derive any assistance from the case of Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills. [186E] (iii) The respondent had no authority to make any claim against the old State of Dholur. [186F] (iv) The respondent did no more than make a claim against the new sovereign. [186G] (v) The respondent 's claim was not justified. [186H] (vi) The respondent claimed the refund of the proportionate export duty for the quantity of 10,427 maunds and 20 seer which he could not export. [186C]

The appellants who were dealers in cotton and groundnuts, were required to take out licences under the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, for the sale of cotton and groundnut. The appellants were required to pay certain fees for the grant of licences. The licence was granted to the appellants on the condition that they would pay the fees for the licence. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder, and the High Court dismissed the petitions. The appellants came to this Court by certificate. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of section 5(4)(a) of the Act were void to the extent it conferred on the Collector authority to refuse a licence at his own discretion and rule 37 was void in so far as it prohibited persons whose names had not yet been registered as buyers and sellers from carrying on business in the notified area. Held, that the provisions contained in section 5(1) of the Madras Commercial crops Markets Act were not void to the effect that the Collector authority was not competent to refuse a license. The provisions of section 14 of the Act did not contravene article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The provisions contained in sections 14 and 15 of the Act, were not void for the reason that they were not reasonable restrictions within the meaning of article 19(6) of the constitution. The provisions in section 14 of Act did not offend article 19(5) of the Consti tution. The provisions were not void in so much as they were not unreasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19 (6) of Constitution. The Act was not void to that extent. The provisions did not contravene the provisions of article 19 of the Constitution as they were unreasonable restrictions within article 19(4)(b) of the Constitu tion. The provisions relating to the grant of licence were not void under article 19(i)(g) and were not unreasonable. The provisions made in section 14 were not void on the ground that they were unreasonable. The Act did not impose any unreasonable restriction on the appellants ' right to carry on their business. The provisions imposed unreasonable restrictions on their right to carry business and were therefore void.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samitis, by a resolution dated April 25, 1973, and was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974, he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975, a resolution was passed by the Panchayat Samithi, which was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 13, 1973. The appellant was appointed on June 1. 1963 by the Gram Panchayat Samiti, which is respondent 3 in this appeal. He was confirmed in the post of Head Clerk on April 1, 1975, in course of the appellant 's service. On March 15, 1975, he was appointed as the Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. The first proviso to section 33(3) of the Act, which was added by the Amending Act of 1973, provided that the persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1, 1973, shall continue to be the employees of the Panchayat Samiti until they were absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. The appellant, who was appointed as an Assistant in the Gram Panchayat, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, asking that he should be absorbed as a Head clerk. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the Amending Act, the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat, on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayat, until he was absorbed in Government Service or retire in the manner prescribed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant 's appointment as a Head Cashier was without the authority of law, and the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post. He was appointed lawfully to the post of a clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. He was, therefore, entitled to be considered for promotion to the post. [738 G H] 2. The appellant had been appointed as a Head Clerks on an ad interim basis in January, 1974, or the subsequent date, namely, January 21,1974, or the date on which he joined the service of Panchayat Samiti, on an ad officiating basis. He was not entitled to be absorbed in the post on the same conditions on which the Government had absorbed him.

HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Aapras of the deity were the personal personal properties of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. [635 D] The High Court has rightly held that the property in question was the personal property and the appellants were entitled to the exemption claimed by them. [636 D] The property in question is the personal property acquired by the Mahant by way of gift or otherwise. The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of land in the village of Raikot in the same district in 1949. Their father was also given quasi permanent allotment in another village in the same District. The two villages were 25 miles or so distant from each other. The two village were 25 miles and so distant from the village. The two other villages were 25 yards or so distant. The appellants filed an application for review of the order cancelling the allotment of land made in their favour in 1949. The Additional Custodian, who was the Deputy Custodian, cancelled the allotment of the land in 1949. On appeal the Additional Custodian held that the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land a had been wrongly fitted in the village Karodian. The Additional Director, who was also the Additional Custodian, held that the appellants were not entitled for allotment of sub urban land a had they been entitled to allotment. The Additional Deputy Custodian, however, dismissed the appellants ' application. The appellants ' revision application to the Custodian General was also dismissed. The appellants then moved the Custodian General for calling up their review application and for revising the order of the Additional Custodian cancelling the allotment. The Custodian General dismissed the appellants application. The Custodian 's revision application was also dismissed by the Custodian General. The appellants came up to this Court by way of appeal. Held, that the Custodian General had no jurisdiction to revise the order of allotment of land. The Custodian had no jurisdiction under the Act to revise the allotment of a land in the absence of any provision in the Act. The Custodian could revise the allotment only on the ground that the allottee or the lessee, as the case may be, had sublet or parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the property allotted to him without the permission of a competent authority or without the permission or with the permission of the competent authority. The Custodian was not a person aggrieved by the order of a competent officer. The Custodian, therefore, had no jurisdiction in the matter.

On January 10, 1942, the Government granted a lease for twenty years to the appellant for a period of 20 years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On December 10, 1947, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah. The Collector, after considering the Board 's report, issued a notice to the appellant to show cause why the lease should not be terminated without any compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant showed cause which, however, did not satisfy the authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh praying for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the Government to forbear from terminating the lease and to forbear the lease. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant came to this Court by certificate. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the second proviso was enacted to nullify the creation of rights in anticipation of the legislation and hence it was not open to the Government to terminate the lease without giving any compensation under that proviso.
